extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (esp. empiricism/epistemology), scholars interested in Hume's critique of innate ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests for deciding whether speculative or practical (moral) maxims are innate; the page lists common proposed marks of innateness and argues against them with examples and counter‑arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assenting as soon as proposed and understood
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that if people assent to a proposition immediately upon hearing and understanding its terms, this immediate assent is a mark that the proposition is innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume rejects this as a proof of innateness: many propositions (mathematical truths, simple contradictories, basic judgments of natural philosophy) receive ready assent as soon as their terms and ideas are understood. Immediate assent shows self‑evidence or clarity once the relevant ideas are possessed, not that the proposition was engraved innately. Examples given: arithmetic ('one and two are equal to three'), 'two bodies cannot be in the same place', 'white is not black'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal assent (general consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that innate principles must have universal assent — everyone who understands them must accept them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues this fails because many supposed maxims do not have universal assent (children, idiots, savages, and large portions of mankind often do not assent). He stresses that innate truths, if real, should be assented to by all who understand them; their absence of universal assent is evidence against innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known before being proposed (present prior to instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard that an innate principle should already be present in the understanding prior to any proposal or teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume contends many people only come to know such propositions when they are proposed; if a truth must be proposed for assent, that suggests it was not actually present innately. He argues that being made clearer by teaching is inconsistent with something being an original imprint of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit knowledge counts as innate
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed distinction that a mind may have implicit (but not explicit) knowledge of a principle prior to its articulation, and that implicit possession counts as innateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume challenges this: 'implicit knowledge' is plausibly only the mind's capacity to form and understand the ideas, not an actual pre‑existing imprinted proposition. He warns against conflating capacity to understand with having an innate propositional impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate truths must be the first thoughts (first principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation that innate principles are the earliest knowledges in the mind — the first that appear when one begins to think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues children and naturals often possess many other ideas and beliefs before any such abstract maxims, so these maxims cannot be genuinely innate since they are not the first objects of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate characters should appear clearest in the least corrupted minds
rubrics_metrics.description: If principles are innate impressions of nature, they should be most evident in those least shaped by education or custom (children, idiots, savages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume notes the opposite: such persons show few or no signs of abstract maxims; hence their absence in these groups is strong presumptive evidence against innateness. He gives ethnographic and observational arguments about the mental contents of 'naturals' and savages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical (moral) principles must operate in action
rubrics_metrics.description: The criterion that genuine innate practical principles should be operative in conduct — they should consistently influence actions, not be mere speculative assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume distinguishes appetites inclinations (desire of happiness, aversion to misery) as innate motives, but denies that moral rules (justice, truth, charity) are innate impressions on the understanding. He argues that if moral principles were innate they would reliably govern behavior; pervasive moral failures and contrary practices indicate they are not innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rules must be self‑evident and need no proof if innate
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that an innate moral principle would be self‑evident and could not reasonably be asked for a reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume counters that moral rules commonly admit of reasoned demand: people ask 'Why must one keep compacts?' and give varying reasons (religion, public utility, honour). That moral rules require proof and differ in rational justification undermines their being innate self‑evident truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as evidence of innate moral principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal that conscience (an internal sense of right and wrong) proves the innateness of moral principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues conscience is itself a form of judgement or opinion formed by education, custom, and reflection; different peoples and individuals have contrary consciences, so conscience does not reliably indicate innate, universal moral truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural universality of moral rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation that innate moral principles would be universally acknowledged across societies and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume provides ethnographic counterexamples (customs that tolerate or practice infanticide, cannibalism, exposure of the sick, differing attitudes to duels, etc.) to show great variety in moral opinions and practices. This variability undermines the claim that moral rules are innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No precedent teaching assumed by immediate assent argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The criticized presumption that assent at first hearing arises without any prior learning or acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume points out the fallacy: even when a person seems to assent without being 'taught', they have in fact learned words, the ideas they signify, and often the relevant observations; thus immediate assent typically presupposes prior acquisition of ideas and names, not innate possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑evidence is not equivalent to innate impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction that a proposition's self‑evidence (being obvious once understood) does not prove it was imprinted innately on the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume accepts that many propositions are self‑evident when understood, but argues that self‑evidence depends on the mind's reflection and the nature of ideas, not on prior natural impressions; therefore self‑evidence does not entail innateness.
